header.title: Fragmenta: AI translation (Claude)
header.author: Eusebius Myndius
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's tlg2640.tlg001.1st1K-grc1, from Open Greek and Latin's First1KGreek (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. The whole work is translated. It was chosen because no English translation of it could be found.
header.statement: An AI-generated translation of the whole work, checked against the original by a second AI only in samples. No specialist has reviewed it.
header.availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's First1KGreek and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg2640.tlg001.1st1K-gr: Section 1: 'of what lies on the opposite side of desire ... may I obtain nothing' renders a difficult clause (τῶν δὲ ἀπ' ἐναντίης τῆς ἐπιθυμίης ...); the text may be faulty, and the negative is taken from μηδέ. Section 1: the printed text runs ἀκέσασθαι ἰδείην with no break, and a new sentence is taken to begin at ἰδείην, read as εἰδείην ('may I know'). Section 1: ίλους is read as Φίλους. Section 2: the last clause (ὑπὸ δὲ τοῦ ... περιτρέψαι ... αἰωρέεσθαι) is awkward and may be corrupt; the rendering is tentative. Section 5: those 'contrary to nature' are apparently people kept or bought as curiosities. Section 15: the rendering takes ἀνύσειε as 'finish off, bring to an end'; the sense is uncertain. Section 16: κτήσι is read as κτήσει. Section 18: Irus is the beggar of the Odyssey. Section 20 has no number in the text as given.

Saying 32 is absent from the text supplied; the numbering runs from 31 to 33. 38: the sentence on the fatherland is awkward, and τοὺς προηγησαμένους may mean either 'forebears' or 'leaders'. 39: the final clause is syntactically strained, as τὰ ... οὐδεὶς ἀνακαλέσεται sits inside the phrase governed by χορηγός; the text may be corrupt, and the rendering is tentative. 45 and 46: δαίμων is kept untranslated. 51: οὐκ ἐόν is taken as 'that you were not'; it could also mean 'something that did not exist'. 54: the 'bond here' is taken to be the bond of vice in this life. 55: ώμην read as ῥώμην ('vigour'), a scanning error.

59: the text's ὅδε μὲν καὶ δὲ appears to be a slip for ὅδε μὲν καὶ ὅδε, translated as "this man and that". ἐγκόψαντες is translated as if ἐγκύψαντες ("looking closely into"). καὶ αὐτοὶ πολυκτήμονες is abrupt and may be corrupt or incomplete; it is taken here as a statement about the complainers themselves. 63: ὄψις ἐούσας διαφανέας ("visions that are clear") is awkward and the sense uncertain. The stray bracket after γῆν has been left out. ἄγει ὁ προειρημένος is obscure, as no object is given. λόγος might also be understood as a personified Word or Reason, here closely linked with Hermes; it is kept as *logos* throughout. The whole passage on the souls' descent and the wall between the two ways is difficult in places, and the construction of ἐπὶ παραγωγῇ ... γεύσασθαι is loose.

nodes.text: 1. May I be an enemy to no one, and a friend to the one who is constant and abides. May I never quarrel with those closest to me, and if I do quarrel, may I be reconciled as quickly as possible. May I plot against no one, and if I am plotted against, may I escape unharmed, without being forced to do anything irreparable in return. May I master anger. May I love and desire and obtain only what is fine, and of what lies on the opposite side of desire, may I obtain nothing, even if I should ever err so far as to pray for it. May I wish all to prosper, and may I envy none of those who prosper. May none of those who are thought to fare well against all reason ever astonish or grieve me; for why should one envy what is given by fortune? And may those who prosper as they deserve be dear to me and gladden me. May I never rejoice at the misfortune of one who of his own will took up enmity against me. May I never be conscious of having been the cause of harm to anyone. If I ever catch myself unawares having said or done something out of tune, may I not wait for those who will find fault and rebuke me, but may I find fault with myself until I have remedied it. May I know how to bear nobly what befalls me, and may I accept moderate misfortunes as their nature is, and to the excessive ones may I not add anything of my own. May I know how to bear good fortune with self-control. May I never be lifted by success into irrational arrogance. May I consider that wealth which suffices for a temperate life. May I never have an unceasing and insatiable desire for money, and may I wish always to reach only for those studies which benefit the soul. May I win the victory that is harmless both to me and to the one conversing with me. May I guard against unseasonable rivalry for honour with friends, and in inquiries too. May I never, in inquiries, embrace strife for the sake of winning, even against what seems right to me. May I never be induced, to the harm of the truth, and against what I myself know, to mislead the one conversing with me or to wrangle. May I always be an ally to the arguments that establish the truth. May I never so much as think of anything belonging to licentious desire. May I always keep company with the temperate, and may it always be mine to converse with those from whom one can certainly come away having gained something useful. May I never be induced to do wrong for the sake of gain. May I reconcile friends who are at odds. May I, when I am able, supply friends, and those in need, with what they need. May I never abandon friends who have fallen into danger, when I am able to help them. May I be eager to set right the misfortunes of friends, by what means are possible; when I am with those who grieve, may I lighten their sorrows with gentle and healing speech. May I know how to feel shame before myself. May I practise a love of learning fine things. May I inquire not into superfluous matters, but into those on which it is best to inquire, and which I shall benefit from learning. May I honour the gods, both by the law of the city and by my own zeal and with a pious mind. May I always tame what is angry in me. May I accustom myself to be gracious, and not to be peevish toward things as they are. Who is wicked, and what has ever been done by any of these, may it be no concern of mine; but may I know the good, and pursue them. May I owe no one anything; but if I am ever brought to this by great necessity, may it be granted me to be able to become free as quickly as possible. May I praise the good without envy, and may I loathe the fault-finding tongue of anyone. May I know how to keep silent on matters where that is better.

2. Men have a greater love of having a reputation for much learning than of speaking the truth. Many, at any rate, by setting up opinions contrary to those of their predecessors, have taken away the knowledge of the truth about the most necessary things, since their credibility does not stand on firm ground; and by turning from their earlier opinion to the contrary, they have arranged for the argument to hover in the most unstable state.

3. Many men, in joint inquiries into matters, are like irrational animals: just as those fight, so these too lay claim only to winning. But as for how this may be done (a thing every man must take forethought for, both in speaking and in acting) without going against the advantage of themselves and those present, and so as not to harm the truth itself, of this they no longer take any account.

4. Quarrels are dear to men, and they have a boundless and irrational desire to want to prevail by contradicting on every subject proposed; since many are not ashamed, even in the most serious matters and those where one should not, to win by the worse argument, winning a victory that deserves to be called Cadmean.

5. Men welcome those who are contrary to nature and count as prodigies, and, buying them for great sums, they rejoice and pride themselves as if on the greatest possession; but on the most serious things they are vexed at spending even small amounts.
6. Most men, who show themselves sparing in everything else and are distressed if they spend anything, gladly throw away even all that they have for the sake of being applauded by the people.
7. Foolish men honour and admire those who have great wealth even when they are worthless, but when they detect poverty in serious men, they look down on them.

8. Consider no one free among those who set their hand to shameful desires; for these men are slaves to masters much harsher than the owners of those who are slaves by fortune, masters who compel them to everything.
9. Gluttony fattens the body and raises up irrationality, but puts to sleep reason, the finest part of the soul.

10. The gods gave man's body to the soul, so that the body should serve the soul. But the many do the reverse, enslaving the better to the worse, the immortal soul to the mortal body, for everything and for its services alone.
11. Licentiousness defiles the soul and destroys the body, which, for the sake of pleasure and in order to be gratified, will compel its possessor to do all the most shameful things.

12. Licentiousness [acts on] the soul as winds on a ship: catching it up and carrying it this way and that, they shake it about and make it disobedient to the helmsman. So too licentiousness, tossing the soul and compelling it to be disobedient to the mind, does not allow it to be at peace and to lie at anchor in the calm and safest place.
13. Love of money does not know how to find a sufficient limit to acquiring.

14. Wealth flowing in day by day does not stop the love of money, just as wood thrown on does not stop a blaze; rather, as it keeps coming, it kindles the desire for more all the more strongly. Mind alone, standing by, knows how to heal this too.
15. Irrational love of money would be brought to an end sooner by the loss of what one acquires than by boundless wealth accruing every day.

16. To manage what one has is the mark of a provident man; but to be wholly unwilling to use it for anything needful is the mark not of a master of what he has acquired, but of one who has enslaved himself to his money by the acquiring.

17. Most men, being sparing beyond reason, think it right, so long as they are believed to be very rich, to be considered silly and gauche rather than to be called clever for spending on what they should.

18. One must consider rich the man who believes he has what suffices; but the man who always desires to acquire more and never gets his fill of wealth, even if he were richer than Midas, I call poor, and I say that he possesses the lot of Irus, which that man had by necessity.

19. Mind embraces truth and always lives with it; but though it is most free of falsehood in what is its own, there are times when it nevertheless mixes falsehood with good and offers it for the benefit of men who need this and who will be misled by it for their own good. For then only and at no other time, and at a moment that it alone knows, mind, though it loathes all other falsehoods, brings in a falsehood of this kind, one changed from the nature of all the other falsehoods into another, most useful form by the art and wisdom of mind itself, which has rearranged a base thing to this end.

Let not a single law in a city allow anyone to lie, no one except the man who loves truth and has intelligence and understands when and how there is benefit in a lie; and the need arising from this makes it necessary to do this too.

21. Frankness comes from a mind that is free and embraces truth; and you will show it to be blameless not by censuring and reviling everyone at random, thinking this to be frankness, but if you speak with good sense to those you should, on behalf of those you ought, and on the occasion you ought, with a view to what is useful, about the matters at hand.
22. An enemy who has told the truth is altogether preferable to a pretended friend who has said everything to please.

23. A man who has great wealth stored away, and then by his own disposition is unable to use it for anything needful, is like one who believes that what is laid up in the public [treasuries] is his own. For in appearance they are equally rich; but of what properly belongs to possession, the use of it, both are equally deprived.

24. A man who has great wealth stored away, and acquires more for this very purpose, and has troubles over how he may always add something to what he has, but spends neither on himself nor on anything else useful, you should never declare to be rich, but a guard and provider of other people's money, and one who chooses to have toils, often acquiring even for those who have no connection with him.

25. This is the proof of the mind of a very good man: not to think that he was born for eating, nor to consider that life consists in this, but to think that food was discovered for men solely for the sake of living.

26. Self-control is a good for the body as well: for it fights as its ally for health, and it gives birth to moderation in the soul. And moderation provides for the soul a state free of strife and calm, and a peaceful life.

27. It is best to accustom oneself to master anger, above all so as not to be easily stirred along by it; but if not that, then at any rate so that you do not at once, and in an unreasoning state, carry out what it compels.

28. Many who think they love themselves do not truly love [themselves]: at any rate, by yielding to themselves in everything for this very reason, and by gratifying themselves contrary to what is right, they fall into the very opposite [of what they want].

29. Many who wish to seem very sound in counsel, when they are called back by those closest to them and of good sense, do not deign to withdraw from what they have once decided, but, so as not to be shown up as abandoning a mistaken opinion, they persist in it, until they actually meet with the evils that come from it.
30. Most people urge men to be true to their oaths; but I declare that it is pious not even to swear readily in the first place.

31. I say that everyone who has formed the intention of swearing falsely and has set out to take the oath, even if he does not complete the act of perjury, through some chance or because the one demanding [the oath] did not wish it, nevertheless has the mind of a false swearer, and is liable for the sin of perjury and for the punishment owed to those who have perjured themselves in deed as well.
33. Idleness wastes the body, and lack of practice in the things that raise it toward what is most godlike [wastes] the soul.

34. Men have got their teeth as a great barrier against light words. But in everything we have need of mind, since if this does not direct the words themselves, they often escape before deliberation, and, disregarding so great a barrier, leap forth unjudged.

35. Anyone who envies a good man in his success envies both his fatherland and the whole community and himself. For a good man in success is the common happiness of the city and of everyone who is able to share in his good fortune.

36. Envy directed against those who are well regarded for the finest things belongs to the idle and ineffectual, but it does not touch the good and those able to bring forth something useful of their own.

37. A man who has much useful learning, and then, being of a bad disposition and not wishing out of envy to share it with those who lay claim to it, is like a bad vessel, which has many good things stored in it and spoils its contents before they come to light.

38. It is a blessing for children to outlive their fathers, and one should ask this of fortune, both for those who will succeed them afterwards, and that each of these in turn, in the order stated, may succeed those before them. But this would be the common and most just prayer, kept by all for the continuance of the greatest thing: that the fatherland, which on each occasion receives and rears all and gave [them] those who went before, should itself, and the established honours of the local gods, always rise to greater excellence.

39. In a city that is to be happy, may wealth never be honoured above virtue, lest for this reason, as all flow together in desire for it, contempt and neglect of the practice of virtue should grow in the souls of those in the city. For when virtue is dishonoured, wealth, alone pursued and holding power, becomes the servant of insolence and arrogance and the provider of all the evils that, through license and the absence of rebuke now that virtue has departed, no one will call back.
40. The respect and honour owed to rulers, when maintained, saves the good order of a city and preserves it.
41. He who presides over and gives orders to others ought to surpass those he commands not only in the authority to preside and give orders, but in worth and judgment.

42. Toward those who live contrary to justice and then claim to lead others, men are disobedient. But everyone who knows how to do his duty earnestly of his own accord, and offers himself as an example of what those under him must do, secures from the governed ready obedience to what is ordered, for himself and for another.

43. This is the only gain proper to a good ruler, and worth ten thousand other gains: to do everything in such a way that both during his time in office and after he has ceased, all good things and justice are attested of him by those he ruled.

44. Let every man, ruler and private citizen alike, know that from the nature of his deeds, of whatever sort he makes them, he will obtain a memory of them of the same sort, either good or bad. And with this in mind let him so decide on which of the roads, the one leading to which of the memories, he should turn, and which of these memories it is better for him to prefer.

45. When you hold office, do not bear a grudge against those who were formerly at odds with you. For you have not been chosen for office so that you may take revenge on enemies, but so that you may keep those placed under you safe and free from plotting by others, and so that you may be a guardian of what is right and a servant and interpreter of a great goddess, Justice. So if you act contrary to what seems good to her and speak falsely against her, as one sinning against a very great goddess, expect wrath for what is done, both from her and from the *daimones* [divine beings] stationed around her as overseers and avengers.

46. When judging between enemies, be an examiner of what is just, and let your verdict incline toward this. For Justice and the *daimon* who oversees her have a juster claim to be honoured above gratifying enmity.

47. If you are in office and then remember enmity, you will assign yourself to the worse lot, and you will deprive yourself of the dignity required in a ruler, and among those who know that you give yourself over to enmity, having taken in exchange for the most dignified names of judge and ruler the name most open to slander, you will be called the enemy of those on trial.

48. I consider that the power to impose the penalty of death on someone lies not in one's having authority to condemn, but in the holder of the power being able to master himself. For even in a judgment that ought to be most secure, if some error is made against those of one's own kind, it is no longer possible to call it back once the error has occurred.
49. What you censure in others as base, first take care not to do yourself.

50. Men come forward to accuse men, some on the basis of concocted false charges, others accusing truly. Others in turn give praise, some attesting what is the case, others gratifying [them] contrary to the truth. So the best thing in such matters, for private citizen and ruler alike, is neither to believe straightaway nor to disbelieve entirely, but from the examination of the facts to learn how one ought to think about them, and the exact truth of them.

51. When you hold office, bring it credit, but do not yourself change. For you have not acquired anything that you were not, nor on ceasing will you have anything less than you had before taking it up, if you lay down the office poor.
52. When you take office, do not be puffed up, but continue the same; for in this way, when you have laid it down too, you will not be thought to have been stripped of anything that lent you dignity.

53. A good man who has taken office over some people or city, not for the sake of enjoying public funds and taking bribes and making money from the rich, is like a man who has received a deposit of great wealth. For just as that man too does not receive it in order to keep it, nor to make what was given his private property, but so as to guard it and return it safe to the depositor when it is demanded back, so he too must do everything not for private gain, but for the safety and protection of those he rules, so that, as far as lies with him, he may return them unharmed and thriving to the one who entrusted them to him.

54. A man who seeks unbearable, savage and immoderate punishments, and is not content with those according to law, giving way to unreasoning passion and growing embittered in womanish fashion, does not perceive that he is committing outrage beyond justice against his own kind. And he is ignorant of the greatest thing, which everyone who is about to condemn a man ought to know: that even death itself was imposed by those who first gave judgment not as an evil, but as a last resort and by way of a remedy for those unable to be freed from vice, so that, since it was not possible otherwise, in this way at least, released from its bond here, they might secure escape.

55. Men who train only strength and vigour and speed, and who are eager that, having these, they may be well regarded for these alone, but do not occupy themselves with care of the soul, fail to realise that they are caring only for these things, which they share with the beasts, and in which they are far weaker than these, while neglecting what is most divine in themselves and that by which it is possible for them, if it can be done, to become like the gods.
56. Praise boldness toward fearful things when joined with reason: for it is courage. But consider an unreasoning rush toward them to be rashness, and detest it.
57. The best harmony in marriage is for both to practise moderation.

58. That gods exist one must not inquire; it is best to have believed it from the outset. For once an inquiry is proposed, even the man who sides with the most impious of arguments, that they do not exist, wants to win.

59. Many people, when they think they are faring worse than they deserve, are indignant, and then, complaining bitterly, say such things as these to themselves and to those around them: "This man marries, and from a prosperous house, but I am unmarried; and that man has a large house and builds magnificently and owns many fields, but I am without a hearth and without property; and this man has plenty of money, but utter want of money holds me; and this man and that hold office and are honoured, but my lot is reckoned as that of a private person without honour." To such people, by way of consolation, one should say that they must not be vexed at the good fortune of others, but be glad of it because of their common kinship; and that they should know that they too are rich in possessions, and that if they look closely into their own circumstances and consider what those others have, they will find that they themselves are faring better; and that no one is deprived of the prosperity owed to him by his neighbour's good fortune.
60. When something painful has befallen, then to be angry with the gods is to seek a greater evil.
61. When something painful has befallen, consider whether it is possible to find anything greater than what is present, and when you have found it, be glad that you have not that, but the lesser.

62. Men demand moderation, which is indeed most necessary, from the women who live with them, and as superiors they think it right to rule their inferiors; but while claiming this, they feel no shame at what is furthest from moderation and from the things that belong to the portion of the superior: they commit these same faults themselves, as if it were allowed to them alone, and they offend thus utterly and without restraint, free from reproach on the women's part.

63. God having shown to the human race from the beginning, according to what is reported, visions that are clear, two ways of life lie before the souls of men, separated from one another at first by an adamantine wall, very thick and reaching to a great height, according to what was [shown] by him who showed [them] from the beginning. One of them, as having been allotted the more honourable station, is on the right hand of those entering; this one leads them to virtue; the other, being on the left, conducts to vice. They are said to be of this kind: the way of virtue seems at first to offer somewhat difficult going, yet such as can be accomplished by continuous toil; but it also has those who guide and escort [travellers] without danger; after this there is a straight and broad road up to the ascent to the acropolis of the beautiful itself; having gone up to it, you will be among the most beautiful things and in the sight of countless other goods, the most blessed ones, and moreover of a light that surpasses all else by infinite beauty and is most radiant. Round about, and over all the land spread out, are the cities and those who inhabit and work the land, concerning whom, how each thing stands, the *logos* [word, reason] sent forth to counsel souls will tell. So this way is somewhat like this; but the one leading to vice is smooth at the beginning, there being very little, and that not genuine but deceptive and meant to lead astray those approaching, for them to taste of what is pleasant; so that, with no guide to be found thereafter, it leads straightway onto a crooked road that has stakes, which are sharp and large and fixed thickly in the ground, and ravines and cliffs, which thrust those travelling headlong down to the river that flows below with mud and stones, which will sweep away and drag off those carried down into it; so that many perish at once in this way, while the rest, by chance and not at all by their own foresight, are scattered to the cities that are there, some to one place, some to another, and over all the country, which is extensive; concerning these too the aforesaid messenger will give an account. These being the ways and such being their nature, the aforesaid leads and stands in the middle, the herald of the great god and counsellor, the *logos*, who proclaims such things as these to the souls about to go down: "Souls of men, whose nature is to be both mortal and immortal, who in what is considered life on earth meet with death, and in what seems death there receive life: when, the time appointed for you having been completed, you are released again from the body that received you in the death there, the lives owed to you will succeed in turn, according to the manner of your life on earth. For this reason I advise you, I the *logos*, prophet and counsellor of the great god Hermes and of the other gods, and to those who disobey I foretell immortal evils, but to those who obey, that there will be goods like those of the gods. You must not, then, for the sake of the briefest, counterfeit and easily scattered pleasure, choose great evils that will remain for all time, and by the briefest life harm the very long life that follows, nor again, in fear of a little toil, give up great goods that will remain for all time and the happiness of the very long life that follows."
